title: Add two registers
summary: Add the two input registers and write the low 64 bits of the sum.
rules: rd is the destination; rs1 and rs2 are the input registers. An input register may also be the destination.
This instruction uses all 64 bits. A result outside the 64-bit range wraps; it does not set condition flags.

examples.explanation: Only the destination is written. Both input registers keep their values.
The first input has every bit set. Adding one produces a bit beyond the register width; only the low 64 bits are stored.

mistakes.explanation: Supply two input registers after the destination.

title: Add a constant
summary: Add a number written in the instruction to an input register.
rules: imm is an immediate: a number written directly in the instruction. It must be from -2048 to 2047.
The immediate is extended to 64 bits by copying its sign bit. The instruction stores the low 64 bits of the sum.

examples.explanation: The negative immediate reduces the input value. The input register stays unchanged unless it is also the destination.

mistakes.explanation: The signed immediate must be from -2048 to 2047. Load a larger constant with li and use add.

title: Add a constant and keep a signed 32-bit result
summary: Add the constant, keep the low 32 result bits, then copy bit 31 into the upper 32 bits.
rules: imm is a number written directly in the instruction. It must be from -2048 to 2047.
The W result is sign-extended to the full 64-bit destination. The upper bits therefore become all zeros or all ones.
An immediate of zero sign-extends the low 32 input bits without changing those low bits.

examples.explanation: The addition sets the retained result’s bit 31. ADDIW copies this bit through the upper 32 destination bits.

mistakes.explanation: The immediate must be from -2048 to 2047. Use a register operation for a larger constant.

title: Add and keep a signed 32-bit result
summary: Add the inputs, keep the low 32 bits, then copy bit 31 into the upper 32 bits.
rules: The W suffix selects a 32-bit result. The input registers are still 64 bits wide.
Copying bit 31 into the upper bits is sign extension. The upper half becomes all ones when bit 31 is one.

examples.explanation: The addition sets bit 31 of the retained 32-bit result. ADDW copies that bit into every upper bit of the 64-bit destination.

mistakes.explanation: Supply both input registers. The W suffix changes the result width, not the number of operands.

title: Keep bits set in both inputs
summary: Write a one at each bit position where both input bits are one.
rules: The operation compares corresponding bits across all 64 positions.
A mask is a bit pattern used to select positions. A one in the mask allows the corresponding input bit to remain set.

examples.explanation: A bit remains set only where both inputs have a one. This selects the input bits allowed by the mask.

mistakes.explanation: Supply two input registers after the destination.

title: Keep bits selected by a constant
summary: Keep an input bit only where the corresponding bit in the constant is one.
rules: imm must be from -2048 to 2047. It is extended to 64 bits by copying its sign bit before the AND.
A negative immediate can therefore have ones in the upper bit positions. Use li and and for a mask this immediate cannot encode.

examples.explanation: The positive immediate has ones in its low eight positions and zeros above them. Only the low eight input bits remain.

mistakes.explanation: The spelling 0xfff is positive 4095, outside the signed immediate range. Use -1 for an all-ones immediate, or load a wider mask into a register.

title: Divide signed integers
summary: Divide the first signed input by the second and write the quotient.
rules: rs1 is the dividend; rs2 is the divisor. Both use the signed 64-bit reading.
The quotient rounds towards zero. Division by zero writes an all-ones result without trapping.
For the most negative signed input divided by -1, the result is that same most negative value. This special case does not trap.

examples.explanation: The quotient of a negative value is rounded towards zero. This differs from an arithmetic right shift when discarded bits are non-zero.
A zero divisor produces an all-ones result. If your program must reject a zero divisor, test it before dividing.
The mathematical positive quotient does not fit a signed 64-bit result. DIV returns the original minimum signed bit pattern.

mistakes.explanation: Supply the divisor register as the third operand.

title: Divide unsigned integers
summary: Divide the first unsigned input by the second and write the quotient.
rules: Both inputs use their unsigned 64-bit readings. A set top bit does not make an input negative.
The quotient rounds down. A zero divisor writes an all-ones result without trapping.

examples.explanation: LI prepares an all-ones bit pattern. DIVU reads that pattern as the largest unsigned value before dividing.
A zero divisor produces the largest unsigned bit pattern. The CPU does not reject the instruction.

mistakes.explanation: Supply the divisor register as the third operand.

title: Load a constant
summary: Ask the assembler to place a constant in a register.
rules: LI is a pseudo-instruction: assembler shorthand that may expand into several machine instructions.
The constant can be a decimal integer or use 0x for hexadecimal. It is not restricted to the 12-bit immediate range of ADDI.
LI constructs a 64-bit constant. Use a minus sign for a negative decimal value; a 0x value describes the stored bit pattern.

examples.explanation: The assembler chooses machine instructions that put the requested constant in the destination.
This constant needs several machine instructions. The after value is captured after the whole LI source line has completed.

mistakes.explanation: The second operand is a constant. Use mv to copy a register.

title: Load an upper constant
summary: Place a constant in bits 31 to 12, clear bits 11 to 0, then sign-extend to 64 bits.
rules: Write the 20-bit constant field from 0 to 1048575, or 0x00000 to 0xfffff. LUI shifts this field left by 12 positions.
Bit 31 of the resulting 32-bit value is copied into the upper 32 bits. LUI does not always create a positive 64-bit value.

examples.explanation: The constant field occupies bits 31 to 12. The low twelve bits are zero.
The constant field sets bit 31. LUI copies that sign bit through the upper half of the destination.

mistakes.explanation: This field needs more than 20 bits. Use li to ask the assembler to construct a larger constant.

title: Multiply and keep the low half
summary: Multiply two registers and retain the low 64 bits of the product.
rules: The low 64 product bits are the same for signed and unsigned multiplication of the same input bit patterns.
The full product can need 128 bits. MUL discards the upper half; use MULH or MULHU when that half matters.

examples.explanation: The destination receives the low half of the product. The input registers keep their values.

mistakes.explanation: The third operand must be a register. Load the constant with li first.

title: Keep the high half of a signed product
summary: Multiply signed 64-bit inputs and write bits 127 to 64 of the 128-bit product.
rules: Both inputs use the signed reading. The H suffix selects the high half of the full product.
Use MUL for the low half. Use MULHU for the high half when both inputs are unsigned.

examples.explanation: The full signed product is negative. Its high half contains the upper sign bits, rather than the small product magnitude.

mistakes.explanation: The third operand is a register, not an immediate constant.

title: Keep the high half of a mixed signed and unsigned product
summary: Multiply a signed first input by an unsigned second input and write bits 127 to 64 of the full product.
rules: The first input uses the signed reading; the second uses the unsigned reading. Swapping their positions can change the result.
Use MUL for the low half. MULH reads both inputs as signed; MULHU reads both as unsigned.

examples.explanation: The first input is negative. The second input’s all-ones pattern is read as the largest unsigned value. The destination holds the high half of that mixed product.

mistakes.explanation: Both input operands must be registers. Load a constant with li first.

title: Keep the high half of an unsigned product
summary: Multiply unsigned 64-bit inputs and write bits 127 to 64 of the 128-bit product.
rules: Both inputs use the unsigned reading. The U suffix changes the meaning of a set top bit.
Use MUL for the low half. Together, separate MUL and MULHU results can represent the full unsigned product.

examples.explanation: The first input has a large unsigned reading. Its full product extends beyond the low 64 bits, so the high half is non-zero.

mistakes.explanation: Load the constant into a register before multiplying.

title: Multiply and keep a signed 32-bit result
summary: Multiply the low 32 input bits, keep the low 32 product bits, then sign-extend to 64 bits.
rules: Sign extension copies bit 31 of the retained result into every upper destination bit. The registers remain 64 bits wide.
MULW discards the product bits above position 31. A later wider operation cannot recover those discarded bits.

examples.explanation: The product’s retained bit 31 is one. MULW fills the upper half with ones instead of retaining the upper half of the full product.

mistakes.explanation: The third operand is a register. Load the constant into a register first.

title: Copy a register
summary: Copy all 64 bits from the input register into the destination.
rules: MV is a pseudo-instruction equivalent to addi rd, rs, 0.
The input register is read, not cleared. Choosing zero as the destination discards the result; that register always reads zero.

examples.explanation: Both registers contain the same bits afterwards. Copying does not remove the original value.

mistakes.explanation: MV copies a register. Use li to load a constant.

title: Invert every bit
summary: Replace each zero input bit with one, and each one with zero.
rules: NOT is a pseudo-instruction equivalent to xori rd, rs, -1.
It inverts all 64 bits. This is a bitwise operation, not the C logical-not operation that produces only zero or one.

examples.explanation: The upper zero input bits also become ones. Inspect the hexadecimal reading as well as the signed reading.

mistakes.explanation: NOT has one input register. Use xor for two inputs.

title: Set bits present in either input
summary: Write a one at each position where either input bit is one.
rules: The operation combines corresponding bits across all 64 positions.
A one in a mask sets the corresponding output bit. A zero in the mask leaves the other input bit unchanged.

examples.explanation: The result combines the set bits from both input registers.

mistakes.explanation: Supply the second input register.

title: Set bits selected by a constant
summary: Set an output bit where either the input bit or the corresponding constant bit is one.
rules: imm must be from -2048 to 2047. Its sign bit is copied into the upper positions before the OR.
A positive immediate affects only its set low bits. A negative immediate can set upper bits too.

examples.explanation: The constant sets a selected bit without clearing the input bits that were already one.

mistakes.explanation: The immediate is outside the signed 12-bit range. Load a wider mask into a register and use or.

title: Find a signed remainder
summary: Write the remainder from signed division of the first input by the second.
rules: The quotient used for the remainder rounds towards zero. A non-zero remainder has the dividend’s sign.
A zero divisor returns the dividend. The minimum signed input divided by -1 has a zero remainder. Neither case traps.

examples.explanation: The remainder follows the dividend’s sign. Combining the quotient times the divisor with this remainder recovers the dividend.
For a zero divisor, REM returns the original dividend. The CPU does not raise a division-by-zero exception.

mistakes.explanation: The divisor is a register operand. Load a constant into a register first.

title: Find an unsigned remainder
summary: Write the remainder from unsigned division of the first input by the second.
rules: Both inputs use their unsigned 64-bit readings. A set top bit contributes a positive place value.
For a non-zero divisor the remainder is smaller than the divisor. A zero divisor returns the dividend without trapping.

examples.explanation: The first input’s all-ones pattern is read as the largest unsigned value. REMU keeps its remainder after division by the second input.
A zero divisor returns the original dividend. Test the divisor before REMU if your program must reject that case.

mistakes.explanation: The divisor is a register operand. Load the constant into a register first.

title: Shift bits left by a constant
summary: Move the input bits left and fill the vacated low positions with zeros.
rules: shamt is the shift amount written in the instruction. For this RV64 instruction it must be from 0 to 63.
Bits shifted beyond position 63 are discarded. Unlike a register-count shift, an out-of-range immediate is not masked to six bits.

examples.explanation: Every set bit moves three positions left. The new low positions contain zeros.

mistakes.explanation: An RV64 immediate shift amount must be from 0 to 63. A shift by 64 needs different code.

title: Compare signed integers
summary: Write one if the first signed input is smaller than the second; otherwise write zero.
rules: Both inputs use the signed 64-bit reading. A set top bit makes a value negative.
The result is an ordinary register value. RISC-V does not put this comparison into condition flags.

examples.explanation: The comparison uses the signed readings. The destination records whether the first input is smaller.

mistakes.explanation: Supply both input registers. SLTI is the explicit instruction name for a register compared with a constant.

title: Compare a signed register with a constant
summary: Write one if the signed input is smaller than the constant; otherwise write zero.
rules: imm must be from -2048 to 2047. It is extended by copying its sign bit before comparison.
Both operands use the signed reading. The destination holds only zero or one.

examples.explanation: Comparing with zero tests whether the signed input is negative. The input register stays unchanged.

mistakes.explanation: The immediate must fit the signed 12-bit range. Load a larger threshold into a register and use slt.

title: Compare unsigned integers
summary: Write one if the first unsigned input is smaller than the second; otherwise write zero.
rules: The U suffix selects unsigned readings. A set top bit contributes a positive place value.
The destination holds zero or one. This comparison can check whether an unsigned addition wrapped by comparing its result with an input.

examples.explanation: The all-ones first input is read as a large unsigned value. The same bits compared with SLT have a different ordering.

mistakes.explanation: Supply both input registers to compare.

title: Shift right while retaining the sign
summary: Move bits right and fill the upper positions by copying the input’s top bit.
rules: shamt must be from 0 to 63. The instruction uses all 64 input bits.
This is an arithmetic right shift. For a negative signed value it rounds down, which can differ from signed division rounding towards zero.

examples.explanation: The input is negative, so the new upper positions contain ones. Discarding low bits rounds this signed result down.

mistakes.explanation: The immediate shift amount must be from 0 to 63.

title: Shift right and fill with zeros
summary: Move bits right and fill the vacated upper positions with zeros.
rules: shamt must be from 0 to 63. Bits shifted below position zero are discarded.
This is a logical right shift. It does not copy the sign bit; use srai when the signed reading must retain its sign.

examples.explanation: The input has every bit set. The shift replaces the top bit with zero, even though the input’s signed reading was negative.

mistakes.explanation: The shift amount must be from 0 to 63. A negative amount does not reverse the direction.

title: Subtract two registers
summary: Subtract the second input from the first and retain the low 64 result bits.
rules: The operand order matters: rd receives rs1 minus rs2.
The result wraps to 64 bits. The instruction does not write carry, borrow or signed-overflow flags.

examples.explanation: The second input is subtracted from the first. Both input registers keep their values.
Subtracting one from zero wraps to an all-ones result. Its signed and unsigned decimal readings describe the same stored bits.

mistakes.explanation: SUB needs two input registers. Use addi with a negative immediate to subtract a small constant.

title: Subtract and keep a signed 32-bit result
summary: Subtract the second input from the first, keep the low 32 bits, then sign-extend to 64 bits.
rules: The operand order is rs1 minus rs2. The upper input bits do not affect the retained low 32 result bits.
Sign extension copies the retained result’s bit 31 into every upper destination bit. SUBW does not write condition flags.

examples.explanation: The subtraction wraps within the retained 32 bits. Their top bit is one, so the upper 32 destination bits are also filled with ones.

mistakes.explanation: SUBW needs two input registers. ADDIW with a negative immediate can subtract a small constant.

title: Set bits where the inputs differ
summary: Write a one where the corresponding input bits differ, and zero where they match.
rules: XOR acts on each of the 64 bit positions independently.
A one in a mask flips the corresponding input bit. A zero leaves it unchanged.

examples.explanation: Positions with different input bits become one. Matching positions become zero.

mistakes.explanation: Supply the second input register or use xori for a constant mask.

title: Flip bits selected by a constant
summary: Flip each input bit selected by a one in the constant; keep the other input bits.
rules: imm must be from -2048 to 2047. Its sign bit is copied into upper positions before the XOR.
An immediate of -1 has every bit set after extension, so it inverts all 64 input bits.

examples.explanation: Only positions selected by a one in the constant are inverted. Other input bits keep their values.

mistakes.explanation: This positive constant is outside the signed 12-bit range. Use li and xor for a wider mask.
